title: Obesity (Sthaulya): Ayurvedic View, Diet & Safe Weight Loss
excerpt: Fat building up around the belly, getting tired quickly, breathlessness and knee pain — obesity is not just about looks, it is the root of many diseases. Learn what obesity is, how Ayurveda understands it as “Sthaulya”, BMI and waist measurement, what to eat and avoid, daily routine, safe home measures and what to be careful about.
content:
“I diet, but my weight still doesn’t come down” or “I lost some in a few months, then gained even more” — many people tell us this at the clinic. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), in 2022 1 in every 8 people in the world was living with obesity, and it is rising fast in India too.

The good news is that with a gradual approach — the right diet, regular exercise and good sleep — weight can be lost safely and kept off. This article is for information only — take any treatment only on the advice of your vaidya or doctor.

What is Obesity?

When the body stores more fat than it needs and this begins to harm health, it is called obesity. There are three simple ways to measure it:

  • BMI (Body Mass Index) — weight (kg) divided by the square of height (metres); for Indians, a BMI above 23 is considered overweight and above 25 obese
  • Waist measurement — a waist above 90 cm in men and 80 cm in women signals belly fat
  • Body shape — especially fat around the abdomen, which is considered the most harmful

Indians tend to carry more belly fat even at a lower BMI, so always check the waist measurement. Obesity raises the later risk of diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, fatty liver, knee wear, snoring and pauses in breathing during sleep (sleep apnoea), and PCOS in women.

The Ayurvedic View

In Ayurveda, obesity is called Sthaulya or Medoroga. Acharya Charaka describes the very obese person (Atisthula) like this:

मेदोमांसातिवृद्धत्वाच्चलस्फिगुदरस्तनः ।
अयथोपचयोत्साहो नरोऽतिस्थूल उच्यते ॥
— Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana 21

Meaning: A person in whom, due to excessive increase of meda (fat) and muscle, the buttocks, abdomen and breasts hang and shake, and whose body has grown but without matching enthusiasm and strength, is called “Atisthula” (very obese).

Acharya Charaka lists eight defects of the very obese person — shortened lifespan, slowness of movement, physical weakness, excessive sweating and body odour, excessive hunger and excessive thirst, and others. According to Ayurveda its root is heavy, sweet, oily food, daytime sleep, lack of exercise and weak dhatvagni (tissue-level digestion), which increase Kapha, ama and meda in the body and block the srotas (body channels). So the aim of treatment is to improve agni, reduce meda and Kapha, and make the body light and active.

Main Causes and Risk Factors

  • Eating more than needed, frequent eating, sweets, fried food, refined flour and junk food
  • Sugary drinks — cold drinks, packaged juices, very sweet tea and coffee
  • Sitting for long hours, lack of exercise, sleeping during the day
  • Staying up late, lack of sleep and stress eating
  • Family history of obesity; low thyroid, PCOS or some medicines (such as steroids) — get these checked by a doctor
  • Weight gained after pregnancy, menopause or quitting smoking that was not attended to

Symptoms and Tests

  • Fat around the abdomen and waist, clothes becoming tight
  • Breathlessness and tiredness on walking a little or climbing stairs
  • Pain in the knees, heels and back
  • Excessive sweating, body odour, itching in skin folds
  • Loud snoring, daytime sleepiness and sluggishness
  • Darkening of the skin on the neck or armpits — this can be a sign of insulin resistance

Before starting weight loss, the doctor may advise thyroid (TSH), fasting sugar or HbA1c, cholesterol, liver tests, blood pressure and, if needed, vitamin D and a liver ultrasound, so that hidden diseases can be detected.

Diet: What to Eat, What to Avoid

In obesity, the aim of diet is to keep hunger balanced, improve agni and slowly reduce total calories. According to Ayurveda, light, dry (low-oil), warm and fibre-rich food is beneficial. Eating right matters, not starving.

What to eat

  • Barley, bajra (pearl millet), jowar, ragi, daliya — instead of refined flour and white rice (in limited amounts)
  • Pulses such as moong, masoor, horse gram and chana, and sprouts — protein keeps you full longer
  • Half the plate vegetables — bottle gourd, ridge gourd, bitter gourd, pointed gourd, cabbage, spinach, salad
  • Less-sweet fruits — guava, papaya, apple, pear (whole fruit, not juice)
  • Lukewarm water, thin buttermilk, unsweetened herbal tea; spices such as ginger, black pepper, cumin, turmeric
  • Eat slowly, chew well, at fixed times; a light dinner 2–3 hours before sleep

What to avoid

  • Sugar, sweets, biscuits, cakes, cold drinks and packaged juices
  • Refined flour, pizza, burgers, noodles, chips, namkeen and fried food
  • Constant snacking, eating while watching TV or mobile, late-night eating
  • Alcohol, too much ghee-butter-cream, and eating when not hungry

Daily Routine and Lifestyle

  • At least 30–45 minutes of brisk walking, cycling, swimming or other exercise every day; increase the time gradually
  • Get up and walk a little every hour; take some stairs instead of the lift, walk for nearby errands
  • Wake early, avoid daytime sleep, sleep by 10–11 pm — too little sleep increases hunger
  • Aim to lose about half to one kilo a week; even losing 5–10% of weight at first greatly helps sugar, BP and the knees
  • Note your weight and waist on the same day every week; set small goals
  • Recognise stress eating — reduce stress with meditation, pranayama or a walk

Yoga

Surya Namaskar, Tadasana, Trikonasana, Bhujangasana, Setu Bandhasana, Naukasana, Kapalabhati and Anulom-Vilom are considered helpful. Caution: with knee pain, back pain, high blood pressure, heart disease, pregnancy or recent surgery, do Kapalabhati and difficult poses only after asking your doctor; if very overweight, start with gentle poses and walking; learn yoga from a trained teacher.

Safe Home Measures

  • Lukewarm water: sip lukewarm water through the day; a glass of water before meals helps balance hunger
  • Honey water: Ayurveda mentions a little honey in lukewarm (not hot) water for Sthaulya — do not take it if you have diabetes
  • Spices: ginger, black pepper, cumin and ajwain in food — for digestion and agni
  • The plate rule: a smaller plate — half vegetables, a quarter dal/protein, a quarter grain

“10 kilos in a week” powders, “fat burner” pills, long fasts or living only on juice can be dangerous — hidden drugs have been found in many such products. These measures are only supportive; the main basis remains diet, exercise and sleep.

Ayurvedic Treatment — With Caution

Ayurveda mentions many medicines for Sthaulya, such as Triphala, Guggulu, Vidanga, Musta, Shunthi (dry ginger) and classical formulations like Navaka Guggulu. Acharya Charaka specially describes Udvartana (massage with dry powder), light food that fills without over-nourishing, and physical exertion for Sthaulya. After examination, when suitable, Udvartana, Panchakarma and the clinic’s diet and lifestyle guidance and yoga and pranayama may be advised. However:

  • Which medicine or procedure, in what amount and for how long — this is decided by the vaidya only after looking at weight, test reports, constitution, pulse, age and current medicines.
  • Do not stop medicines prescribed by your doctor on your own — especially diabetes, BP, thyroid or steroid medicines; as weight falls their dose may need changing, which only the doctor will decide.
  • Some herbs (such as guggulu) can change the effect of other medicines, so tell your vaidya the list of all your medicines; avoid unlabelled “weight-loss powders”.
  • During pregnancy and breastfeeding, and for children, teenagers and the elderly, take any weight-loss medicine or diet only on the advice of a vaidya/doctor. Beware of claims like “guaranteed weight loss without diet or exercise”.

When to See a Doctor Immediately

  • Chest pain, sudden severe breathlessness or fainting — go to a hospital immediately
  • Very rapid weight gain without trying, with swelling of the face or legs
  • Pauses in breathing during sleep, loud snoring and excessive daytime sleepiness
  • Excessive thirst, frequent urination, or high sugar/BP reports
  • Dizziness, severe weakness, heavy hair loss or periods stopping while dieting
  • Strong guilt about food, vomiting after eating or repeated uncontrolled eating — seek help for mental health too

Summary — Points to Remember

  • Check waist measurement along with BMI — belly fat is the most harmful
  • Don’t starve — right, light, fibre-rich food at fixed times
  • Daily exercise, walking a little every hour and full sleep
  • Lose weight slowly — half to one kilo a week; avoid miracle powders
  • Medicines and Panchakarma only under a qualified vaidya; don’t stop current medicines on your own
